lines.text: Every atom in your body is almost entirely empty space.

lines.text: How small is an atom, really?

phrases.text: How small is an atom, really?

lines.text: Start with a single human hair, about seventy micrometers wide.

phrases.text: Start with a single human hair, about seventy micrometers wide.

lines.text: Ten red blood cells, side by side, would just span it.

phrases.text: Ten red blood cells, side by side, would just span it.

lines.text: Each of those cells is about seven times wider than a bacterium.

phrases.text: Each of those cells is about seven times wider than a bacterium.

lines.text: A virus is roughly ten times smaller still.

phrases.text: A virus is roughly ten times smaller still.

lines.text: Inside your cells, DNA is a strand just two nanometers wide.

phrases.text: Inside your cells, DNA is a strand just two nanometers wide.

lines.text: And an atom? About a tenth of a nanometer.

phrases.text: And an atom?

lines.text: It would take half a million atoms, side by side, to cross that one hair.

lines.text: But here's the strange part: an atom is almost entirely empty.

lines.text: Scale one up to the size of a football stadium, and its nucleus would be a grain of sand on the center spot.

lines.text: The electrons? Just a faint haze, out in the stands.

lines.text: Everything in between is empty space.

phrases.text: Everything in between is empty space.

lines.text: Including the atoms that make up you.

lines.text: Does knowing you're mostly empty space change how you see yourself? Tell me in the comments.
